traveler: Paul the Deacon (Paulus Diaconus, Paulus Warnefridi)
title: The Deacon of a Finished Kingdom: Cividale, Pavia, Benevento, and the Mountain
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, the ancestor who came with Alboin
stops.date_confidence: attested as a claim, unverifiable as an event. Paul himself reports the descent in Historia Langobardorum IV.37, on the authority of his elders, two centuries after the fact; the migration of 568/569 under Alboin is independently attested, the Leupchis filiation is not. Dated to the migration year, which is where Paul puts it.
stops.campa: Paul will one day write his own family into the history of his nation, in the fourth book, on the authority of his elders: Leupchis, who crossed into Italy with King Alboin in the year of the migration and settled in Friuli, and the generations after him down to Warnefrid, the father of the man holding the pen. It is a handful of sentences inside a long chronicle. No other Lombard of the eighth century puts his own grandfathers into the national record, and because this one does, a Friulian household of the sixth century has names.
suggested_refs: Historia Langobardorum IV.37, the family digression
The Lombard migration of 568/569 under Alboin
sources: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum IV.37, cited in Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, the birth in Forum Iulii
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No birth record exists. Lidia Capo (Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani) places the birth 'probably between 720 and 730'; English Wikipedia says 'about 720'. The year 725 here is a midpoint used to order the segment, not an attested date. [A] the parents Warnefrid and Theodelinda and the Friulian origin; [R] everything about the date.
stops.campa: In Forum Iulii, seat of the first Lombard duchy planted in Italy, a son is born to Warnefrid and Theodelinda. The family keeps its own descent by heart: Leupchis, generations back, crossed the Alps with King Alboin and took land in Friuli. The boy will be called Paulus, and after his order Paulus Diaconus, and after his father Warnefridi, which later readers turn into a birth name of his own and give him as Winfrid. He grows up in a walled town on the Natisone, a day's ride from the Avar frontier, in a house where the crossing is still spoken of as something that happened to relatives.
suggested_refs: Lidia Capo, 'Paolo Diacono', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
The Lombard walls and river gorge of Cividale, ancient Forum Iulii
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Aquileia, the education that did not happen
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and near-impossible. Popular lives credit Patriarch Calixtus of Aquileia with directing Paul's first studies; Lidia Capo finds no proof of it. Worse, Calixtus held the see 726-734 (en.wikipedia, 'Patriarch of Aquileia'), so a boy born c. 720-730 was at most nine when he died. Recorded here as a false tradition about Paul, not as an event in his life.
stops.campa: On the lagoon edge sits the patriarchal basilica, metropolitan church of the province, its floor a fourth-century sea of mosaic fish. A tradition long repeated in popular lives has the patriarch Calixtus taking the boy from Friuli in hand and directing his first studies. Calixtus held the see from 726 to 734, and spent what energy he had on moving the patriarchal residence up to Cividale. A child born around 725 would have been nine at the outside when the patriarch died.
suggested_refs: The mosaic pavement of the basilica of Aquileia
Lidia Capo's rejection of the Calixtus tradition, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, Santa Maria in Valle: the sister who wept
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and weak. The Tempietto Longobardo is dated to the mid-eighth century and credited to Duke Astolfo and Giseltrude (it.wikipedia, 'Tempietto longobardo'); that page says nothing whatever about Paul or his family. The identification of his sister's convent with this building is modern popular biography. [A] the sister and her grief, from Paul's own petition poem; [R] the house she entered.
stops.campa: Above the gorge of the Natisone stands a small square chapel of stucco and vine scroll, six saints in relief along one wall, raised in the middle of the century by the duke Astolfo and Giseltrude. Later biography puts Paul's sister here, the unnamed woman vowed to Christ from girlhood whom he mourns in the poem to Charlemagne, weeping until she is nearly blind. Paul never names the house she entered. The chapel is the finest Lombard building still standing in the town.
suggested_refs: The Tempietto Longobardo (Santa Maria in Valle), Cividale
Versus Pauli Diaconi ad regem Karolum precando, on the weeping sister

segments.name: The Palace School on the Ticino

stops.name: Pavia, the road to the royal palace
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Capo places the move into the palace milieu 'probably under King Ratchis' (reigned 744-749); Wikipedia says 'probably at the court of the Lombard king Ratchis in Pavia'. No document records the move, its date, or who arranged it. Coordinates are the historic centre of Lombard Pavia, inherited byte-identical from charlemagne.journey.json; the palace footprint is not archaeologically fixed.
stops.campa: The road west out of Friuli ends at the brick capital on the Ticino, where the Lombard kings keep their palace, their mint, and their schools. Paul enters that household as a young man, in the reign of Ratchis, who will abdicate in 749 to take the habit at Monte Cassino. Nothing records who brought him or on whose word. He will spend the better part of thirty years inside this world, learning what the palace has to teach: grammar, the Latin poets, and the rudiments of a Greek the court needs for its dealings with Byzantium.
suggested_refs: The Lombard royal palace quarter at Pavia
Ratchis, king 744-749, later monk of Monte Cassino
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Pavia, Flavian's grammar and four syllables of Greek
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, undated as to the year. Flavian is named as Paul's master only in Ilderic's acrostic epitaph, written a generation after Paul's death. The self-deprecation is Paul's own, in the verse letter to Peter of Pisa; the Latin says the syllables were learned 'in scolis', in the schools, which locates them here rather than in boyhood Cividale.
stops.campa: His master is the grammarian Flavian, named in the acrostic epitaph Ilderic composes for him a generation after he is dead. In the schools he is set at Greek and at Hebrew, the two languages a Latin grammarian is expected to be able to gesture at. He learns, by his own accounting, three or four syllables of each, and goes on saying so in verse for the rest of his life, politely, in front of the men who praise him for languages he does not have. I know no Greek speech, he writes, and I am ignorant of Hebrew.
stops.quote: Graiam nescio loquellam, ignoro Hebraicam. / Tres aut quattuor in scolis quas didici syllabas
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, verse reply to Peter of Pisa ('Sensi cuius verba'), thelatinlibrary.com/pauldeacon/carmina.shtml
suggested_refs: Ilderic's acrostic epitaph of Paul, Monte Cassino
Pauli et Petri Diaconorum carmina, ed. Duemmler, MGH Poetae Latini aevi Carolini I (1881)
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Pavia, the order that gives him his name
stops.date_confidence: unresolved contradiction, flagged not settled. Capo calls the ordination date unknown and infers a Pavian diaconate before Monte Cassino from the contemporary form of address, which is an argument from silence, so [R]. English Wikipedia states flatly 'ordained as deacon around 782', i.e. after Monte Cassino and at the Frankish court, reversing the sequence. The 755 here is an ordering device for the first reading and nothing more.
stops.campa: Contemporaries address him as Paulus levita, Paul the deacon, and the title sticks so hard it becomes his surname in every catalogue after him. When he took the order, and from whose hands, nobody wrote down. The Italian record puts it here, at Pavia, in the court years, before he ever sees Monte Cassino. A strand of the English tradition puts it forty years later, around 782, in Francia. The two accounts reverse the whole sequence of his life, and there is no document either way, only the form of address.
suggested_refs: The contemporary designation 'Paulus levita' in the Carolingian letter collections
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Pavia, in the household of King Desiderius
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to role, attested as to milieu. Later tradition calls Paul secretary or chancellor to Desiderius; no appointment document survives and Paul never claims a title. Capo and Wikipedia agree on the association with the court and disagree on nothing except how formal it was. Date is an ordering device inside Desiderius's reign (756-774).
stops.campa: Under Desiderius, last king of the Lombards, Paul is close enough to the palace that later writers make him the king's secretary, or his chancellor. No appointment survives; nothing in his own writing claims a title. What is visible is the work: verse for the royal house, the education of the king's daughters, and a familiarity with the court's business that will let him describe a palace from the inside twenty years after it has stopped existing. He is in the household, and no document says on what footing.
suggested_refs: Desiderius, king of the Lombards 756-774
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Isola Comacina, the praise of the Larian lake
stops.date_confidence: the poem is attested, the residence is not. 'Versus in laudem Larii, Comensis laci in Italia' stands among the six poems on the Latin Library's carmina page. One sentence in English Wikipedia adds that Paul 'entered a monastery on Lake Como' before Monte Cassino; Capo's fuller account knows of no such house. Coordinates are Isola Comacina, the lake's principal early monastic site, used as a marker only. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: He writes a poem in praise of the Larian lake, its clear water and its fish and its oil, one of six pieces of verse to come down under his own name. A late strand of the record turns the poem into a residence and puts him in a monastery on Como years before he ever goes south. The fuller Italian account knows nothing of any such house. The island in the middle of the lake, Comacina, holds the oldest monastic settlement in the region, and that is where the story is set when it is told at all.
suggested_refs: Versus in laudem Larii, Comensis laci in Italia
The early monastic settlement on Isola Comacina

stops.name: Benevento, the princess brought south
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the marriage, reconstructed as to Paul's arrival. 'Around 757, Arechis married Adelperga, a daughter of the northern Lombard king Desiderius' (en.wikipedia, 'Arechis II of Benevento'); he became duke in 758. Wikipedia's Paul page says only that he lived at the Beneventan court 'for at least several years before 774'. The year of his own move south is nowhere recorded.
stops.campa: Around 757 Desiderius marries his daughter Adelperga to Arechis, who becomes duke of Benevento the following year. She goes south with a household, and Paul goes with it, or joins it soon after, as her teacher and her reader. The Beneventan court is Lombard as Pavia is Lombard, but out of Frankish reach, five hundred miles down the peninsula with the Apennines set between. For something like fifteen years the most learned Lombard alive works for a woman who reads Eutropius in the evenings and complains that he leaves things out.
suggested_refs: Arechis II, duke and later prince of Benevento
Paul's preface to the Historia Romana, addressed to Adelperga
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Benevento, Santa Sofia raised on a star of columns
stops.date_confidence: attested for the building, silent as to Paul. 'Arechis II of Benevento constructed the church around 760' (en.wikipedia, 'Santa Sofia, Benevento'), whose coordinates are used here. The page does not name Paul, and no document connects him to the fabric; his relation is to the patron and the household, not the building.
stops.campa: Arechis raises a church on a strange plan, a star of six columns set inside a decagon, and calls it Holy Wisdom after the great church of the Byzantines whose rival he intends to be. It is a dynastic building: a duke who cannot be king at Pavia builds a Constantinople in miniature in the south. Paul's name appears nowhere in its fabric; he belongs to the household that pays for it and writes its epitaphs. The columns are spoils, carried in from older temples and stood on end under the new roof.
suggested_refs: Santa Sofia, Benevento, and its Lombard fabric

stops.name: Benevento, the poem whose initials are a name
stops.date_confidence: unverified, and flagged as such. The acrostic chronological poem 'A principio saeculorum' is credited to Paul, with initials said to spell 'Adelperga pia' and a date of 763, on the strength of Duemmler's MGH Poetae Latini I (1881). The specialist catalogue geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3884 gives only a general 'Carmina' entry dated broadly c. 750-799, with no acrostic and no year, and the poem is absent from the Latin Library carmina page. Neither the acrostic nor the year could be confirmed in this pass.
stops.campa: A chronological poem runs through the ages of the world from the creation forward, and its opening letters are said to spell the name of the princess it is made for. It belongs to the same tutorial relation as everything else he produces at Benevento: history handed to a reader who asked for it, arranged so that the arrangement itself is the compliment. Whether the initials read Adelperga pia, and whether the thing was finished in 763, are claims the nineteenth-century editions carry and the working catalogues decline to repeat.
suggested_refs: Ernst Duemmler, ed., Pauli et Petri Diaconorum carmina, MGH Poetae Latini aevi Carolini I (1881)
geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3884

stops.name: Benevento, sixteen books for a reader who wanted more
stops.date_confidence: attested as to commission and content; the endpoint is disputed. geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3890 dates composition 'um 766-774' and gives the scope as a world chronicle 'um 565', a continuation of Eutropius into the time of Justinian; Wikipedia gives 766-771, and the dossier's original endpoint of 552/553 is not supported. The endpoint is best stated as 553 or c. 565, variously. More than 160 manuscripts survive.
stops.campa: Adelperga has read Eutropius and found him thin. He stops short, and he says nothing of sacred history, and nothing of the emperors who matter. Paul takes the Breviarium apart and rebuilds it, threading scripture and church history through the pagan annals and carrying the story past the end Eutropius made for it, down into the age of Justinian. Sixteen books. It becomes the standard Roman history of the middle ages, copied in more than a hundred and sixty manuscripts, and it exists because a Lombard princess in Benevento wanted a better book than the one she had.
stops.quote: Eadem Adelperga monente Paulus grandius opus suscepit, historiam Romanorum ab Eutropio scriptam augendam et continuandam
stops.quote_source: Editorial summary in Bethmann and Waitz, MGH, Scriptores rerum Langobardicarum et Italicarum saec. VI-IX (1878). This is the editors describing Adelperga's prompting, not Paul's own dedicatory letter.
suggested_refs: Amedeo Crivellucci, ed., Pauli Diaconi Historia Romana, Fonti per la storia d'Italia 51 (1914)
geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3890
sources: archive.org OCR of MGH, Scriptores rerum Langobardicarum (scriptoresreruml00paul_djvu.txt)

stops.name: Benevento, the bones under the altar
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Paul's authorship of verse praising the translation of the relics of St Mercurius to Benevento under Arechis II is carried from the research dossier and was not verified against a primary source in this pass, so [R]. The coordinates are inherited byte-identical from saint_mercurius.journey.json, whose own stop notes that no reached source dates the arrival of the relics; if Paul praised the translation, it belongs in Arechis's reign, before 787. Year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Bones come into Benevento under the name of Mercurius, the soldier-saint of Cappadocia, and are laid under an altar. Arechis is the prince who brings them, and Paul, in the household that writes the prince's verse, praises the translation. Nobody at Benevento is deceived by anybody. Eleven centuries later the bones will be separated out and identified as those of a different Mercurius, out of Aeclanum, a local saint absorbed into a famous file by the ordinary process that swallows small names into large ones.
suggested_refs: saint_mercurius.journey.json, 'Benevento, the relics that are not his'
Hippolyte Delehaye on the Mercurius of Aeclanum
sources: Research dossier on Paul the Deacon (Arechis II as patron), unverified against primary text

stops.name: Salerno, the walls and the new palace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the building programme, reconstructed for Paul's verse. Arechis 'put resources into building projects in Salerno, including a new palace and castle' (en.wikipedia, 'Arechis II of Benevento'). Coordinates are the historic centre of Salerno per en.wikipedia, 'Salerno'; an earlier pin at 40.6746, 14.7663 fell in the harbour and is discarded. The hilltop Castello di Arechi is popularly credited to Arechis, but its own article says his intervention there was 'practically nonexistent'.
stops.campa: Arechis puts money into Salerno: new walls, a new palace, a seaside town treated as a second capital for a principality that has stopped calling itself a duchy. Paul writes verse for the programme, setting the Christian city his patron is raising against the plundered grandeur of old Rome. The hilltop castle above the town, which local tradition hands to Arechis whole, is barely his at all. What is his is the wall line down in the city, and the palace standing inside it.
suggested_refs: The Lombard walls of Salerno and San Pietro a Corte
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castello_di_Arechi, disputing the popular attribution

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the habit taken
stops.date_confidence: unresolved, flagged not settled. Capo reads Ilderic's epitaph as framing the conversion as the culmination of Paul's Lombard career, which puts it before 774; Wikipedia says only 'before 782 he entered the great Benedictine house of Monte Cassino'. The date 772 orders the segment on Capo's reading and asserts nothing. Wikipedia additionally suggests Paul met Charlemagne at Monte Cassino rather than in Francia, which the fuller Italian account does not support; the discrepancy is left standing.
stops.campa: The abbey on the mountain above the Liri, refounded sixty years earlier on the ruin Benedict left, takes him as a monk. Ilderic's epitaph sets the conversion at the end of a long Lombard career rather than at its collapse, which would put it before the Franks ever came over the Alps; other accounts have him arriving afterward, a man of a finished kingdom looking for a house that will hold him. The mountain has taken Lombard royalty before. Ratchis, the king whose palace school he entered as a boy, ended here in the habit.
suggested_refs: Ilderic's acrostic epitaph of Paul
The abbey of Monte Cassino under abbot Petronax and after
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Pavia, the capital opens
stops.date_confidence: attested for the event, blank for Paul. The siege and fall of Pavia in 773-774 are independently attested and are two stops in charlemagne.journey.json, from which this pin is inherited byte-identical. No source of any kind places Paul at Pavia in 774, and Capo says his location during the siege is unknown.
stops.campa: Charlemagne sits down in front of Pavia through the winter and starves it, and in June the brick capital opens. Desiderius goes into a Frankish monastery; the iron crown changes hands; the kingdom of the Lombards, two hundred and six years old, stops existing as a thing a man can serve. Where Paul is that month, no source says. His king is gone, the southern court he writes for survives by paying tribute, and the chancery Latin he was trained in belongs from this year on to foreigners.
suggested_refs: charlemagne.journey.json, 'Pavia, the siege of the Lombard capital begins' and 'Pavia falls: the Iron Crown of the Lombards'
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, Hrodgaud's revolt and the brother taken
stops.date_confidence: attested. Duke Hrodgaud of Friuli revolted in 776 and Charlemagne suppressed it. The captivity of Paul's brother Arechis and the family's ruin are attested by Paul himself in the petition poem, whose text was confirmed verbatim at thelatinlibrary.com. Paul's own participation in the revolt is documented nowhere; only his brother's captivity is.
stops.campa: Hrodgaud, duke of Friuli, rises against the Franks in the second year of the occupation. Charlemagne comes over the mountains, kills him, and empties the duchy of its leading families. Paul's brother Arechis, who carries the same name as the prince of Benevento, is taken north into Francia as a captive. The household goods are carried off, such as they were. A family that counted its descent from Alboin's crossing is turned out of its nobility and into begging in one season, and seven years later Paul will still be counting from this.
suggested_refs: The revolt of Hrodgaud of Friuli, 776
Versus Pauli Diaconi ad regem Karolum precando
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the clerics sent up from Naples
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, undated. The Gesta episcoporum Neapolitanorum records that Bishop Stephen of Naples sent clerics to study at Monte Cassino under 'Paul the deacon'; the text was not fetched directly in this pass and reaches this file through Capo. The year is an ordering device inside abbot Theodemar's tenure. Wikipedia's Monte Cassino article independently names Paul among the notable monks of the period.
stops.campa: Under abbot Theodemar he becomes the abbey's teacher, and the reputation of the school travels down the roads into Campania. He is around fifty, a monk of a suppressed kingdom, living under a rule in a house that was a heap of stones within living memory. Stephen, bishop of Naples, sends his own clerics up the mountain to study with Paul the deacon. The Neapolitan book of the bishops records it in a single line, the way it records any ordinary arrangement.
suggested_refs: Gesta episcoporum Neapolitanorum
Abbot Theodemar of Monte Cassino
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono', citing the Gesta episcoporum Neapolitanorum

stops.name: Rome, Saint Peter's: the meeting that may not have happened
stops.date_confidence: hypothesis, not event. Wikipedia and the dossier both float a first meeting between Paul and Charlemagne at Rome during the king's Easter visit of 781; the dossier itself calls it 'possible but not certain', and no source places Paul in the city. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from charlemagne.journey.json, whose own Saint Peter's stop is dated to Easter 774, not 781. Recorded here as a guess historians make because the timing is convenient.
stops.campa: Charlemagne comes to Rome for Easter in 781 and has his sons anointed by Pope Hadrian. Historians put Paul on those steps because the timing is convenient: the king's later willingness to hear a Lombard monk out has to begin somewhere. Nothing places him in the city. The petition is still a year off, and when it comes it reads like a first approach to a stranger. Did the two men meet here, or does the acquaintance begin only when the poem reaches the king's hands?
suggested_refs: charlemagne.journey.json, 'Rome, Saint Peter's, Easter: the king climbs the steps on his knees'
The Easter visit of 781 and the anointing of Pippin and Louis

stops.name: The itinerant Frankish court, the petition put into the king's hands
stops.date_confidence: attested for the poem, unfixed for the place. The Latin text is headed 'ca. 782' at thelatinlibrary.com and its lines were confirmed verbatim. The court in 782 was itinerant in the Rhine, Moselle and Saxon theatre; the Aachen palace chapel was not begun before 793 and the complex not before c. 796, so Aachen is anachronistic as a building. The coordinates are the palace-school pin from charlemagne.journey.json, inherited byte-identical and used as a conventional marker for 'the Frankish court', not as a claim that Paul stood at Aachen. The poem runs 27 lines in the Latin Library text, an impossible count for continuous elegiac couplets; the dossier's '28 lines' is dropped as unverified.
stops.campa: He goes north with his abbot's leave and puts a short poem in elegiac couplets into the king's hands. The verse does not argue policy and asks for no principle. It says the seventh year is at hand since the disaster came on the family. It says his brother is in Frankish country, naked and in need. It asks the king to look with a calm face on a servant's words and with pity on his weeping. Every device the palace school at Pavia taught him is aimed at one domestic transaction: the release of a single prisoner out of the several hundred a rebellion produced.
stops.quote: Verba tui famuli, rex summe, adtende serenus, / Respice et ad fletum cum pietate meum!
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, Versus Pauli Diaconi ad regem Karolum precando, c. 782, thelatinlibrary.com/pauldeacon/carmina.shtml
suggested_refs: Versus Pauli Diaconi ad regem Karolum precando, full Latin text
charlemagne.journey.json, the palace-school stop

stops.name: The itinerant Frankish court, the inventory of the ruin
stops.date_confidence: attested. All four details, the captive brother, the wife begging with a trembling mouth, the four children, the sister nearly blinded by weeping, and the seized household goods, were confirmed line by line in the Latin text at thelatinlibrary.com and cross-checked against Bibliotheca Augustana. The dossier's version of the impoverishment couplet fused two non-adjacent lines; the couplet quoted here is the real one, lines 21-22. Date is an ordering device within the same spring.
stops.campa: The poem inventories the ruin item by item. The captive's wife begs food through the streets of her own town with a trembling mouth, and holds four children up by that trade. A sister, vowed to Christ since girlhood, has nearly wept herself blind over the same misfortune. The household goods, however little they came to, were carried away. Nobility ended and want came in on the wretched, he writes, and then, in the very next line, that they had deserved to suffer harder things than these.
stops.quote: Nobilitas periit, miseris accessit egestas; / Debuimus, fateor, asperiora pati.
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, Versus Pauli Diaconi ad regem Karolum precando, lines 21-22, thelatinlibrary.com/pauldeacon/carmina.shtml and Bibliotheca Augustana
suggested_refs: Bibliotheca Augustana, pau_carm.html, for the line numbering

stops.name: The itinerant Frankish court, the letter that calls it a prison
stops.date_confidence: attested, dated by the letter itself. Capo confirms the letter to abbot Theodemar of 10 January 783, including its substance: the grace not yet granted, Paul confined at the palace, longing to return. The place within the itinerant court is not fixed; see the coordinate note on the preceding stop.
stops.campa: On the tenth of January he writes back to the mountain. The grace has not been granted. He is kept at the palace, honoured and fed and consulted, and he tells his abbot the place is like a prison to him and that he means to come home shortly. He is the most admired Latinist at the court of the man who ended his kingdom and took his brother, honoured by that man in front of everybody, and he is writing south to a Benedictine abbot to say he wants out. He will stay another three years.
suggested_refs: Paul the Deacon, letter to Abbot Theodemar, 10 January 783
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: The itinerant Frankish court, the epitaph for the child Hildegard
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the poem, inferred as to the month. 'Epitaphium Hildegardis filiae' stands among the six poems on the Latin Library carmina page. Hildegard was Charlemagne's infant daughter, named for her mother the queen, and died in 783; the month is an ordering device. The dossier had this as an unverified lead and tagged it [R]; it is upgraded here to attested on the strength of the Latin Library listing.
stops.campa: Queen Hildegard dies in 783 and the infant daughter who carries her name dies in the same year. Paul writes the child's epitaph. He is composing the royal family's grief for them, in formal Latin, in the same season in which his own family is still waiting on the king's answer about a prisoner nobody at the palace has mentioned again. It is court work, of the kind a household poet supplies without being asked twice, and it is one of only six poems that come down under his name in the manuscripts.
suggested_refs: Epitaphium Hildegardis filiae, in the Paul the Deacon carmina

stops.name: The itinerant Frankish court, the exchange with Peter of Pisa
stops.date_confidence: attested for Paul's side, corrected for Peter's. Paul's verse reply is confirmed verbatim at thelatinlibrary.com. The dossier's claim that Peter compared him to Homer, Horace and Virgil and asked him to teach Greek is NOT in en.wikipedia, 'Peter of Pisa', which instead quotes Peter, writing as Charlemagne's amanuensis, calling him 'most learned of poets and bards' sent 'to our back-water, as shining light with the various languages you know', and dates the riddling exchanges 782-786. The Homer-Horace-Virgil detail is dropped. Year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Peter of Pisa, writing at the king's dictation, sends him verses calling him the most learned of poets and bards, a shining light brought into a backwater, a man of many languages. Paul answers that he knows no Greek and no Hebrew, that he picked up three or four syllables in the schools, and that he has no gold, no silver and no purse to send back, only affection. The riddling exchanges, verse letters and puzzles going both ways, run on across the court from 782 to 786.
stops.quote: Sensi, cuius verba cepi exarata paginis, / Nam a magno sunt directa, quae pusillus detulit
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, verse reply to Peter of Pisa, thelatinlibrary.com/pauldeacon/carmina.shtml
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_of_Pisa
Ernst Duemmler, ed., Pauli et Petri Diaconorum carmina, MGH Poetae Latini aevi Carolini I (1881)

stops.name: Metz, the bishops in order and the ancestor found
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the commission and the content, unconfirmed as to presence. Bishop Angilram of Metz commissioned the Liber de episcopis Mettensibus, edited and translated by Damien Kempf (Dallas Medieval Texts and Translations 19, 2013). Whether Paul travelled to Metz or composed it elsewhere in the Frankish orbit and sent it is not established by anything fetched. Coordinates are Metz cathedral per en.wikipedia. Chrodegang's episcopate 742-766 is confirmed there.
stops.campa: Angilram, bishop of Metz and arch-chaplain to the king, asks him for a history of the see, and Paul produces the first serious book of its kind north of the Alps: the bishops of Metz in order from the beginning, with Chrodegang, who brought the Roman chant and the Roman liturgy into the city a generation earlier, standing near the end of the line. Into that succession he fits Arnulf, and out of Arnulf he runs the descent down to the reigning king. A Lombard of a conquered kingdom supplies the Franks with their holy ancestor.
suggested_refs: Damien Kempf, ed. and trans., Paul the Deacon, Liber de episcopis Mettensibus (2013)
Chrodegang of Metz, bishop 742-766
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Corbie, fifty-four letters of Gregory sent to Adalard
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, presence unconfirmed. The Corbie connection, a collection of fifty-four letters of Gregory the Great sent to Adalard and a mention of travel in the district, comes from Paul's own letter collection through the dossier; en.wikipedia, 'Corbie Abbey' does not name Paul at all. Adalard's dates conflict inside Wikipedia itself: the Corbie article gives him as ninth abbot 780-824, while en.wikipedia, 'Adalard of Corbie' has him exiled to Noirmoutier in 817, restored after seven years, and dead 2 January 827. Written here as abbot from c. 780, exiled 817 to c. 824, died 827. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from ratramnus_of_corbie.journey.json.
stops.campa: Adalard governs the abbey on the Somme, a cousin of the king's and master of one of the great Frankish schools. Paul sends him a collection of fifty-four letters of Gregory the Great, gathered and corrected, the kind of gift that moves a text out of one library and into another and thereby keeps it alive. He mentions travelling in the district in a later letter. Whether he ever stood inside the enclosure itself, the correspondence does not settle.
suggested_refs: The Corbie scriptorium and its Carolingian hand
The Registrum of Gregory the Great and its Carolingian transmission

stops.name: Monte Cassino, back inside the enclosure
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the return, approximate as to the month. Capo places the return to Monte Cassino and the southern Italian sphere no later than autumn 786. The fate of the brother is not recorded either way; the sources simply stop mentioning him.
stops.campa: By the autumn of 786 he is back in Italy and back on the mountain. Four years north: verse for the royal household, a history for Metz, letters to Corbie, and the standing of the most cited scholar at a court he arrived at as a supplicant. Whether he ever got his brother out, no document says; the record simply stops mentioning the brother. Theodemar is still abbot. Paul is about sixty when he goes back under the rule, and he will not leave the enclosure again.
suggested_refs: Abbot Theodemar's Monte Cassino in the 780s
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

segments.name: The Mountain and the Late Books

stops.name: Salerno, the epitaph for Arechis
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the death and the epitaph, uncertain as to the place. Arechis II died on 26 August 787; en.wikipedia, 'Charlemagne' independently confirms that he 'fled to a fortified position at Salerno before offering Charlemagne his fealty', and the Arechis article notes that the exact place of death is not explicitly stated. Paul's epitaph 'Lugentum lacrimis populorum' is well attested and confirms that he was again in the southern Lombard orbit.
stops.campa: Charlemagne marches into the duchy of Benevento; Arechis pulls back to the fortified place at Salerno and offers his fealty; and on the twenty-sixth of August he dies. Both of Paul's patrons are finished now, the northern king by conquest and the southern prince by death. For the prince who married Adelperga thirty years earlier and gave him a court to write in, the monk of sixty on the mountain composes an epitaph that opens on the tears of the peoples.
suggested_refs: Lugentum lacrimis populorum, Paul's epitaph for Arechis II
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arechis_II_of_Benevento
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, a pope assembled out of libraries
stops.date_confidence: attested as to authorship and sources, broader as to date than the dossier claimed. geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3891 dates the Sancti Gregorii Magni Vita to c. 782-787, spanning the Frankish years, so 'shortly after his return from Francia' is unsupported narrowing; the year here orders the segment only. Confirmed there: the sources are Gregory's own writings, Gregory of Tours's Decem libri historiarum, and Bede; a ninth-century expanded recension added legends; over 100 manuscripts survive.
stops.campa: He writes a life of Gregory the Great out of Gregory's own books, out of Gregory of Tours, and out of Bede: a pope assembled from libraries because there are no witnesses left to ask, two centuries on. It is the earliest full life of Gregory to survive, and the pope in it is the pope of the writings, the administrator and the letter-writer, rather than the wonder-worker. A ninth-century hand will pad it out with miracles, and it is that swollen version, not his, which travels through more than a hundred manuscripts with his name on the front.
suggested_refs: geschichtsquellen.de/werk/3891
The two recensions BHL 3639 and BHL 3640
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, Festus cut down a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the work and the dedication, approximate as to date. Dating c. 786-799 per geschichtsquellen.de/autor/4242; standard edition W. M. Lindsay, Sexti Pompei Festi De verborum significatu quae supersunt cum Pauli epitome (Leipzig, 1913). Composition at Monte Cassino is probable rather than documented.
stops.campa: Sextus Pompeius Festus had abridged Verrius Flaccus in twenty books on the meanings of words, and the copy on the mountain is damaged and getting worse. Paul cuts the abridgement down again, one epitome standing on another. Later scholarship will call it a mutilation, and it is also the only channel through which most of what Festus preserved of the old Roman vocabulary reaches anybody at all. He dedicates the finished epitome to Charlemagne, king of the Franks and of the Lombards.
suggested_refs: W. M. Lindsay, ed., Sexti Pompei Festi De verborum significatu cum Pauli epitome (1913)
geschichtsquellen.de/autor/4242

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the homiliary the king put into law
stops.date_confidence: attested as to commission and authorization, approximate as to completion. Charlemagne requested the two-part homiliary and authorized its dissemination with a prefatory Epistola generalis; the late 790s dating and the scale of its circulation follow Zachary Guiliano, The Homiliary of Paul the Deacon (Brepols, 2021), described at brepols.net and not read directly in this pass.
stops.campa: The king wants the night office read from decent texts and asks him to assemble them. Paul goes through the fathers and lays out a cycle of sermons in two parts, winter and summer, running the length of the church year, and Charlemagne issues a letter authorizing its use throughout the realm. It is the most widely copied thing he ever makes and the least personal: a lectionary in which his own voice does not appear at any point, imposed by decree on churches from the Elbe to the Ebro.
suggested_refs: Zachary Guiliano, The Homiliary of Paul the Deacon (Brepols, 2021)
Charlemagne's Epistola generalis

stops.name: Monte Cassino, six books nobody commissioned
stops.date_confidence: attested as to authorship and place, bracketed as to date. Wikipedia dates the Historia Langobardorum after 787 and no later than 796, 'maybe at Montecassino'; Capo notes Book I must be earlier than 796 because it speaks of Avar dominion as still current. Paul names himself as a monk of the monastery in Books I and VI. No patron is recorded for the work.
stops.campa: He begins the last book, the one nobody asked him for. Six books on the Lombards, from an island in the north to the death of Liutprand, written inside a monastery of a kingdom that no longer exists, by a man whose own forefather crossed the Alps with Alboin. It is a history of the defeated composed under the protection of the victor, and it carries no complaint anywhere in it. He writes while the Avars still hold the plain he describes them holding, which fixes the first book before 796.
suggested_refs: Historia Langobardorum, Books I and VI, where Paul names himself
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Langobardorum
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Scadinavia, the island that sends out a third of itself
stops.date_confidence: narrated geography, not an itinerary. Paul never went north; this is the legendary setting of Historia Langobardorum I.1 and I.8, pinned conventionally in southern Scandinavia so the narrative's northern reach appears on the map. The Foulke translation's own footnotes debate whether 'Scadinavia' meant the peninsula at all. The date is the composition period, not an event date. Text confirmed verbatim at elfinspell.com on two fetches.
stops.campa: The history opens in the far north, on an island called Scadinavia, where the cold breeds men faster than the ground can feed them. The Winnili divide by lot into three, and the third that draws the short lot has to leave. Paul argues the demography flatly: the north is healthy because it is cold, and healthy peoples overflow. Then he tells how the god Godan named the Winnili at a window, their women's hair bound down over their faces to look like beards, and how Frea got the victory for the people she had got the name for. He calls it a silly story, worthy of laughter, to be held of no account, and writes it in anyway.
stops.quote: The region of the north, in proportion as it is removed from the heat of the sun and is chilled with snow and frost, is so much the more healthful to the bodies of men and fitted for the propagation of nations...
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum I.1, trans. William Dudley Foulke (Philadelphia, 1907), text at elfinspell.com
suggested_refs: Historia Langobardorum I.1 and I.8, Foulke translation
The Godan and Frea naming legend and its Origo Gentis Langobardorum parallel

stops.name: The march out of Scoringa, the dog-headed men in the camp
stops.date_confidence: narrated geography, not an itinerary, and the pin is notional. Scoringa, Mauringa and the Assipitti cannot be securely mapped; older identifications with the Elbe, the Baltic or the Usipetes are conjectural, and Paul's immediate written source is not securely identified either. The coordinates are a conventional placement in the North European Plain so the episode appears on the map at all. Text of I.11 confirmed verbatim at elfinspell.com. Date is the composition period.
stops.campa: Between Scoringa and Mauringa the Assipitti block the road, and the Lombards are too few to force it. So they put out a rumour. There are Cynocephali in the camp, men with the heads of dogs, who fight without stopping, drink human blood, and drink their own if they cannot reach the enemy. Paul reports the dog-headed men as what they are in his own telling, a story spread on purpose by a small force in a tight place. The tents go up wide and a great many fires are lit, so that the camp looks like an army from outside, and the Assipitti go home.
stops.quote: They pretend that they have in their camps Cynocephali, that is, men with dogs' heads. They spread the rumor among the enemy that these men wage war obstinately, drink human blood and quaff their own gore if they cannot reach the foe.
stops.quote_source: Paul the Deacon, Historia Langobardorum I.11, trans. William Dudley Foulke (Philadelphia, 1907), text at elfinspell.com
suggested_refs: Historia Langobardorum I.11, the Assipitti stratagem
ratramnus_of_corbie.journey.json, the Epistola de Cynocephalis, for the theological branch of the same motif
san_cristobal.journey.json and megasthenes.journey.json, for the classical and hagiographic branches

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the history stops at Liutprand
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the breaking-off point, open as to why. The narrative ends at the death of King Liutprand in 744, thirty years before the fall of the kingdom. Whether this was a deliberate choice or the work was left unfinished at Paul's death is a live scholarly dispute, flagged rather than resolved. Date is an ordering device inside the composition window.
stops.campa: The narrative stops at the death of Liutprand in 744, thirty years short of the fall of the kingdom and well inside the century Paul himself lived through. Whether he chose to end where the Lombards were still whole, or whether death took the last books off him, has been argued for two hundred years and cannot be decided from the text. He names himself in the first book and again in the sixth as a monk of this monastery on this mountain. There the Lombards stop.
suggested_refs: The unfinished ending of the Historia Langobardorum, Book VI
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the day without a year
stops.date_confidence: day attested, year reconstructed. The Monte Cassino necrology records the death on the Ides of April and gives no year; modern reconstructions range 797-799, and Capo notes an alternative tradition of 21 July. The conventional 799 rests on the argument that Paul appears to have died before Charlemagne's imperial coronation at Christmas 800. The Latin quoted here follows the necrology text cited in it.wikipedia, 'Paolo Diacono'; the dossier's 'venerandus memoriae' is ungrammatical and the MGH page carrying the notice could not be reached, the archive.org OCR truncating short of it.
stops.campa: He dies on the Ides of April, in the abbey, an old man. The house records it in its book of the dead without a year, as it records everyone: on the Ides of April died lord Paul, deacon and monk, of venerable memory. The year has to be argued backward out of silence. He appears nowhere after the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor at Christmas 800, and a writer of his standing would have been asked for something on that occasion, so the reckoning puts him dead before it. One tradition gives the day as the twenty-first of July instead.
stops.quote: Eidus aprilis. Obiit venerandae memoriae domnus Paulus diaconus et monacus.
stops.quote_source: Necrologium Casinense, as quoted in it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Diacono
suggested_refs: The Monte Cassino necrology
Bethmann and Waitz, MGH, Scriptores rerum Langobardicarum (1878), introduction
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, beside the church, before the chapter house
stops.date_confidence: later Cassinese tradition, [R]. The Latin is 'iuxta ecclesiam Sancti Benedicti, ante capitulum', beside the church of St Benedict and in front of the chapter house, not inside the church as one paraphrase has it. No securely identifiable grave survives; the abbey was destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly and levelled by bombardment in 1944. Italian Wikipedia states plainly that later rebuildings 'hanno cancellato ogni traccia della sua tomba'.
stops.campa: Cassinese tradition puts him in the ground beside the church of Saint Benedict, in front of the chapter house, where the community would pass him every morning on the way in. The abbey is sacked, thrown down by earthquake, rebuilt, thrown down again, and flattened by aerial bombardment in 1944. Later rebuildings erased every trace of the tomb. No cult formed around him, no canonization was sought, and no relic was ever claimed. Nothing on the mountain marks him now.
suggested_refs: The successive destructions and rebuildings of Monte Cassino
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Monte Cassino, Ilderic writes the acrostic
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The acrostic epitaph attributed to Ilderic is probably early ninth century; its authenticity has been questioned without being decisively overthrown. It is the principal near-contemporary narrative source for Paul's court upbringing, his study under Flavian, and his monastic conversion. The date is a conventional placement in the early ninth century.
stops.campa: A generation after his death someone in the house, named in the manuscripts as Ilderic, writes an acrostic epitaph for him: the court upbringing, the grammarian Flavian, the conversion to the habit. Nearly everything anybody knows about the first fifty years of Paul's life comes through this one poem, and its authenticity has been doubted for a century without being overturned. The man who wrote his nation's history out of what his elders remembered is himself known mainly from a poem written after he was dead.
suggested_refs: Ilderic's acrostic epitaph of Paul the Deacon
sources: Lidia Capo, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Paolo Diacono'

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, Codex XXVIII comes home
stops.date_confidence: manuscript attested, arrival date unknown. en.wikipedia, 'Historia Langobardorum' lists 'Cividale del Friuli, Museo Archeologico Nazionale, XXVIII' among the manuscripts, and the museum's own site refused connection on every attempt in this pass. The codex is early ninth century; when it reached Cividale is not established, and the date here orders the segment only. Manuscript census: about 115 copies per Laura Pani (2000); the oldest is the late eighth-century Assisi palimpsest of Books II and V; the earliest complete copy is Codex Sangallensis 635, Waitz's base text. Coordinates are the historic core of Cividale, matching the birth stop; an earlier pin at 13.426 fell some 450 m west of the museum.
stops.campa: A copy of the Historia Langobardorum made within a generation or two of his death ends up in the town he was born in, and is still there, catalogued as Codex XXVIII in the archaeological museum on the cathedral square. The history of the Lombards comes back to the first Lombard duchy in Italy, a few hundred paces from wherever the house of Warnefrid stood. There are about a hundred and fifteen manuscripts of the work altogether; the oldest is a palimpsest fragment at Assisi, and the oldest complete one is at Saint Gall.
suggested_refs: Cividale del Friuli, Museo Archeologico Nazionale, Codex XXVIII
Laura Pani's manuscript census of the Historia Langobardorum (2000)
Codex Sangallensis 635; the Assisi palimpsest

stops.name: Monte Cassino, the hymn that names the notes
stops.date_confidence: legend, [R], and layered on centuries late. The attribution of 'Ut queant laxis' to Paul is first securely traceable to twelfth-century Cassinese writers, Alberic and Peter the Deacon, and is repeated by Durandus c. 1286; no eighth or ninth-century witness names him. The lost-voice story is theirs, not his. Guido of Arezzo's use of the hemistich initials in the eleventh century is independent of the authorship question and is not in dispute. Date 1100 marks the first secure attestation of the attribution, not an event in Paul's life.
stops.campa: Twelfth-century writers on the mountain tell it this way: Paul lost his voice before he was to sing the Holy Saturday reading, and composed a hymn to John the Baptist asking to have it back. A century before those writers, Guido of Arezzo had taken the first syllable of each half-line of that hymn and made the names of the notes out of them, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. The attribution to Paul cannot be traced back past the twelfth century. Whether he wrote the hymn the scale is named after, nobody has been able to establish.
suggested_refs: Canterbury Dictionary of Hymnology, 'Ut queant laxis'
Guido of Arezzo and the solmization syllables; the seventh syllable added c. 1592-1600, variously credited to Ludovico Zacconi or to Anselmo of Flanders

stops.name: Cividale del Friuli, a square with his name on it
stops.date_confidence: modern, undated. The Piazza Paolo Diacono in the Borgo San Domenico quarter of Cividale was located by OpenStreetMap Nominatim geocoding; the date of the naming is not established and the year here is a placeholder to put the stop last. Several searches failed to confirm any statue or bust of Paul in the town; only the square name is verified.
stops.campa: In the Borgo San Domenico quarter of Cividale there is a square with his name on it. That is the whole of the commemoration that could be confirmed: no statue found, no bust, no birth house pointed out to visitors, a paved space and a sign. The critical Latin text of his history was printed at Hannover in 1878 and the standard English one at Philadelphia in 1907, and neither city ever saw him. The museum a few streets from the square holds the ninth-century copy.
suggested_refs: Piazza Paolo Diacono, Borgo San Domenico, Cividale del Friuli
Ludwig Bethmann and Georg Waitz, eds., MGH, Scriptores rerum Langobardicarum et Italicarum (Hannover, 1878)
William Dudley Foulke, trans., History of the Langobards (Philadelphia, 1907; rev. Edward Peters, 2003)
